Editorial

Marianne Parsons and Ann Horne

Ann Horne

Ann Horne  

Readers will be interested to know that there are a number of changes concerning the Journal, some of which have already happened, some about to happen.

Sue Kegerreis’ term of office as Editor ended in December 1992, and as the new Joint Editors we want to record our thanks to Sue for her hard work and commitment to the Journal over the last few years.

We are also very pleased to announce that from January 1994 the Journal of Child Psychotherapy will be published by Routledge. Routledge will be undertaking an intensive international marketing drive, especially in the USA, Europe and Australia, which should result in increased circulation. Not only will journal papers, as a result, be read more widely, but we hope that the profession of child psychotherapy itself will also benefit from the Journal being more in the public eye.

As we move to Routledge as publishers, we will also be undertaking a major move to publishing three times per year: issues will appear in March, July and November. Information about this and the subscription changes which it will entail to non-members of the Association of Child Psychotherapists will be circulated in the near future.

We are planning a Special Issue for the first (March) 1994 number. This will focus on Autism and will feature two exciting papers by Frances Tustin. Authors interested in contributing to this are still welcome to submit, but papers need to be with us by 30th September 1993.

To coincide with the publication of the Journal by Routledge, we are proposing to form an Editorial Advisory Board of internationally well-respected names. We also plan to appoint additional overseas representatives. Further details of these developments will be announced in the near future.

We look forward to the changes ahead and to the ongoing growth and development of the journal as a forum for debate and professional expertise. We continue to welcome your ideas and thoughts, and above all your papers which enable child psychotherapists to share theory, practice, innovation and technique internationally.

responseSet.abstract:
[[RunningHead]]

The Damaged Identity Tag: A Prematurely Terminated Analysis of a Latency Boy**

Cynthia Carlson

Cynthia Carlson

The Anna Freud Centre
21 Maresfield Gardens
London NW3 5SH.

Cynthia Carlson  

Hugo was referred to the Centre at the age of 8 by his doctor, because he suffered both day and night from the fear of being “taken away” by an ostrich. The initial diagnostic hypothesis was of a typical infantile neurosis, but it became evident early on that the neurotic superstructure masked a more profound narcissistic disturbance with associated problems in structuralisation, integration and sense of self. Hugo treated others as extensions of himself and related exclusively to his primary objects and their substitutes with a limited capacity for concern (Winnicott 1963). He was absorbed with beating fantasies which served in place of missing ego functions, including control of drive discharge, defence against painful affect and stabilisation of self-cohesiveness. Hugo was locked in a Sado-masochistic relationship with his mother which was especially frightening due to the lack of separateness he experienced in relation to her. His sense of omnipotence, which was fuelled by parental handling, was a major source of resistance.

This paper looks at the 17-month analysis which gradually focused on the preoedipal tie to mother, as it became apparent that it was here that the impasse in his development lay. The analysis was characterised by a double resistance from both mother and son, and was prematurely terminated by mother when separation issues came to the fore in our work.

Referral

Although Hugo's other serious problems were mentioned by his parents in their description of him, such as his friendlessness and unhappiness, these were glossed over, the ostrich fear being the main presenting problem, largely because it had spread to the point where Hugo's anxiety had begun to rule the household. Hugo was afraid to stay alone on any floor of their large house for fear the ostrich might appear. He got his mother to sit with him while he did his homework in the evening, and again while he fell asleep, a routine which took hours. Hugo ended up spending most of every night in the parental bed, and MrP complained they had no evening life as a couple. Mrs P agreed, linking her over-protectiveness to the time when Hugo needed special attention at 2 years because of his frequent illnesses, which resulted in him “now being too strongly attached to me”.

[[RunningHead]]

Attachment and Psychotic Processes in an Anorexic Adolescent**

Barbara Segal

Barbara Segal

Great Ormond Street
London WC1.

Barbara Segal  

Introduction

This paper describes a crucial aspect in the drive towards death which manifested itself in the treatment of a severely anorexic 14 year old girl, Amelia. I pay considerable attention to the early part of treatment as this enables one to trace, with hindsight, the mechanism used by my patient to avoid psychic pain of one kind. As treatment progressed her wish to die increased, hospitalisation was necessary to keep her alive and yet her investment appeared to be in the analytic process and her relationship with me. Her idealisation of me and of psychotherapy worked against her recovery and opened the way for perverse and destructive forces to take hold, resulting in an acute psychotic illness. Amelia's passionate involvement in the therapeutic encounter caused great anguish at the end of each session and she formed an allegiance and attachment to anti-life and anti-hope constructs, i.e. to a perverse object-relationship. The limits of psychotherapy resources in the NHS setting meant that Amelia could only be seen once a week, increasing to twice a week.

Attachment

Attachment theory is described as a way of “conceptualizing the propensity of human beings to make strong affectional bonds to particular others and of explaining the emotional distress and personality disturbance, including anxiety, anger, depression and emotional attachment, to which unwilling separation and loss give rise” (Bowlby 1977).

Attachment behaviour seeks to create a tie which binds one person to another, it includes crying and calling, which elicit care, following, clinging and also protest when left. The intensity of attachment may be heightened or diminished by situational conditions: for example, helplessness and defencelessness bring fear for survival, and in such a state of terror attachment to a destructive part of the personality may be formed. Turning towards or becoming attached to a therapist may create this danger at the moment of separation.

Pearl King and Richardo Steiner, Eds. The Freud-Klein Controversies 1941-45. London, Routledge, 1991. £100 (Hardback).

Michael Fordham

Michael Fordham

Michael Fordham  

This formidable volume covers the crisis that arose in the British Psycho-Analytical Society that was largely brought about by the vigorous attack on Melanie Klein's work by members of the Viennese group headed by Anna Freud, with the addition of Edward Glover and Melita Schmideberg (Melanie's daughter). It is an interesting and informative book, especially because it documents the tendency for developments in psychoanalysis to proceed by rifts in which one or more psychoanalysts are either expelled or retire from the main body headed by Freud. It all started with the direct or indirect expulsion of Jung, Adler, Stekel and their associates; it seems that comparable processes have been and continue to be repeated, especially in the United States.

Belonging to a ‘dissident’ tradition that Jung initiated, I find it all especially interesting because there have been similar splits having, if I am not mistaken, comparable causes: a main one being the assertion by a number of ‘true blue’ analysts that a deviant theory and practice had arisen which should no longer be called ‘Jungian’ or ‘Freudian’. In the case of the analytical psychologists in London a smaller number of analysts broke off to start an alternative training which was supposedly ‘true blue’; that splitting again to make four training groups in all. Whereas the Society of Analytical Psychology had not succeeded in containing the two groups, the psychoanalysts had done so. Would this very detailed exposition shed any light on why different theories and practices raised such intense and even violent emotions?

The first section of this massive volume is headed “The evolution of controversies in the British Psycho-Analytical Society”. It begins with a valuable editorial introduction by Pearl King and goes on to record a series of Extraordinary Business Meetings, the first of which was held on February 25th 1942. In this and subsequent meetings the discussions consider a number of resolutions proposing changes in the constitution. It seemed to be agreed that changes were desirable because of the tendency of officers to remain in their posts for too long and so form a kind of oligarchy; but there were differences about how and when to make them. Was it justified to do so at a time when so many members had joined the army, or were occupied in contributing to the war effort in other ways so that they could not attend meetings? Was it desirable to initiate changes in the constitution before the ‘scientific’ discussions proposed had defined the outcome of conflicting theories? These and other matters occupied five meetings in all.

[[RunningHead]]

Mustn't Bite the Hand That Feeds: The Boy Who Refused to Eat

Bret Koplow

Bret Koplow

7345 Medical Center Drive, Suite 150
West Hills, California 91307, USA

Bret Koplow  

An unremarkable diet had characterised Aaron E.'s nine years of life, that is, until a few months prior to intake. During that period, no solid food had passed Aaron's lips and his sustenance had become entirely dependant upon liquid nutritive supplements. His teeth had begun to decalcify; his weight had begun to drop, though not with such significance as to warrant a diagnosis of Anorexia Nervosa. Although several presenting problems were enumerated by his mother on the application for service, including separation anxiety and low self-esteem, only “DOES NOT EAT’ was printed in capital letters as well as underlined three times. Aaron's refusal to eat was clearly his mother's greatest conscious concern.

Background Data

At intake, Aaron was a nine year old Caucasian of Jewish parents. His only sibling, a brother three and half years older, was described by Aaron and his parents as having “no problems”. Both parents were employed, his father as a skilled professional, his mother as a secretary at both Aaron's school and her own parents’ small business. Both were college educated.

Self and parental reporting emphasised Aaron's social and athletic skills. His grades and IQ fell within the average range. Recent eating patterns had not diminished his academic, social or athletic performances.

Both sets of grandparents resided in the local area. Aaron's mother, in fact, was employed by her own parents and the family received additional financial support from her parents as well as from the paternal grandparents. There was, however, a frequently expressed resentment within the family that the father's parents did not provide the appropriate amount of financial support. This expectation existed despite a family income well above average. Additionally, the family owned their home as well as rental property in an affluent neighbourhood of Los Angeles. As should be apparent, issues of dependency were highly visible among both parents.

Aaron's brother had been born prematurely and Aaron, when born jaundiced, created panic in his mother who worried she would not be able to take her new son home. Eleven months of breast feeding as well as subsequent weaning occurred without incident. Intermittent enuresis was demonstrated until approximately age five.

This valuable collection of papers presents a view of the expanded practices and interests of child psychotherapists and child analysts. The contributions of 28 practitioners have been grouped under the headings: 1. Patients, families and treatment approaches. 2. The psychotherapy of infancy. 3. Patients treated in adolescence. 4. Special areas of work. 5. Theory and research.

The richness and variety of years of experience and work in the field is reflected in the editors’ choice of subjects and material. The papers are highlighted and linked very helpfully by Rolene Szur. The editors pay tribute to the Child Guidance multidisciplinary approach and to the forum provided by the Journal of Child Psychotherapy, both of which have contributed to the application of psychoanalytic thinking to different sorts of work. It is generous and appropriate that the royalties from this book will go to the Child Psychotherapy Trust to ensure further training of child psychotherapists to work with children and families within the NHS.

Corinne Aves  

This is an enriching, eclectic collection of papers edited by an educational psychologist with a strong interest in psychoanalytic approaches to the understanding of children. The contributing authors include child psychotherapists, psychiatrists, bereavement counsellors and psychologists, all of whom offer highly individual perspectives on children with particular constellations of vulnerability.

The theme of a “secret life” to be recognised and understood in working with vulnerable children is a useful one and serves to unify the varied professional perspectives. The idea that there are underlying processes, confusions, conflicts, something hidden to be engaged with in the children we meet in our professional work is not likely to be accepted as axiomatic amongst the average multi-disciplinary team. However, such thinking is bread and butter to child psychotherapists. There is more than a passing similarity between the notion of “secret life” and Melanie Klein's concept of an “internal world”. Indeed the child psychotherapists among the authors interpret secret life in this way. However, there is also scope for more systems oriented approaches in terms of family secrets, scripts, interpersonal dynamics and socio-cultural factors to enrich our view of what is obscure to us in our patients.

Children may be vulnerable by constitution, as a result of trauma, neglect, or disability, or they may be passing through particular stages of development which render them more vulnerable than usual.

Obsessionality, Communication and Mis-Communication**

Patsy Ryz

Patsy Ryz

36 Essex Park
London N3 INE

Patsy Ryz  

This paper is an account of the first 2 years of therapy with an adolescent boy whom I shall call Leonard. He was referred to the clinic, aged 16, for compulsive, obsessional behaviour which affected his whole functioning and was having a particularly crippling effect on his school work. Having been a “straight A” student, he was now re-sitting exams in order to attain the standard required to enable him to go on to more advanced studies. Initially I saw him 3 times a week but in the 2nd year this was reduced to twice weekly. This is not a theoretical paper and there is no theoretical overview; it is a clinical account of the process of the therapy. As implied by the title, the focus is on the changing nature of the communication, its relation to the obsessionality and the way these changes and fluctuations parallel the development of the therapy.

Leonard's thinking processes had come to a virtual standstill due to the setting up of an obsessional system designed to spare him any experience of psychic pain. The material thus offers an opportunity to chart his gradual emergence from the stranglehold of obsessionality into the freer regions of creative thinking and “true” - i.e. meaningful communication.

The Stranglehold - Obsessionality as Communication

At the start Leonard's obsessionality was pervasive and all-encompassing, contaminating any contact between us. It was thus a powerful communication through which I learned a great deal about the quality of his relationship to his objects and about the objects themselves.

Quite early on it became apparent that Leonard's internal world was dominated by a bullying taskmaster; an internal dictator who imposed rituals and compulsions in exchange for “protection” from worries and anxieties. The price for this was heavy, namely the paralysis of all thinking processes; a kind of mental constipation.

The start of therapy was particularly difficult for Leonard. He was very tense and nervous - unable to tolerate even the slightest pause in our conversation. This manifested itself in an uncomfortable, pasted-on smile which threatened to erupt into nervous giggling. Leonard found this extremely distressing. Eye-contact too was nerve wracking, but its avoidance was equally tormenting. The following notes, made at the initial assessment, give a picture of him at this time.

Limits and Structure in Child Group Psychotherapy

John Woods

John Woods

21 Hillfield Road
London NW6 1QD.

John Woods  

The Internal Group

The number of patients seen by a therapist, say in a day, or rather those who are alive in the therapist's mind, make up a group. Though they may never meet each other they may also be alive in each other's mind. Some days therefore I have an interesting “group” consisting of a boy aged 12 struggling with bi-sexuality, a Bosnian refugee raging about his internal war, a rock musician who finds he can only relate to others from on a stage, a family with an anorexic teenager and a pregnant woman with a history of bulimia. These people relate to each other only through me, as I am the therapist for each of them; however, the therapeutic contact that each has is affected by what I choose to take up, not just with that one but with all, and by the way I respond to them all. Just as the heart of psychoanalytic psychotherapy is the quality of relationship between therapist and patient so is the state of mind of the therapist profoundly influenced by his experience of all his patients. These internal groupings are not limited by time or by any other external constraint such as compatibility of one to another. One of any therapist's patients may be in this way crucially related to someone who was worked with by that therapist, perhaps years before.

When patients are introduced to each other in actuality the therapist cannot predict what transpires. The therapist has no control over the significance each patient may have for another. The balance of power shifts dramatically. Thus we tend to speak of a “member” of a group rather than a “patient”. So if we play within the rules of external reality we must be more circumspect about whom we introduce to each other. There are no rules about group psychotherapy which will necessarily predict which combinations will be therapeutic or not. Experience shows that there are patterns of likely eventualities rather than rules, and there is a body of theory that conveys much of this experience. Group Analytic theory provides a model that integrates the intrapsychic with the interpersonal. There is not space here to summarise all of Foulkes’ work and that of his followers, Foulkes (1948, 1964), Foulkes and Anthony (1965), but I propose in this paper to refer to some of the concepts of Group Analysis in relation to my efforts at working with groups of children in recent years.

[[RunningHead]]

The Starving and the Greedy: Inner and Outer Objects in Anorexia Nervosa

Christopher Dare

Christopher Dare

De Crespigny Park
London SE5

Christopher Dare  

Introduction

In a previous publication (Dare, 1988) a schematic account of a family therapy with a young anorexic patient was presented in order to depict a psychoanalytic psychiatrist's approach to family therapy. This present paper continues an exploration of the families and the family therapy of anorexia nervosa integrating a psychoanalytic viewpoint with that of family systems theory. It is not an account of a distinctive, that is to say a ‘pure’, psychoanalytic family therapy of the eating disturbance. Rather, by making an extended account of a case in treatment, further details of the integrated model can be described.

There is an extensive literature on family organisation and structure in anorexia nervosa (e.g. Dare, 1985; Minuchin et al., 1975, 1978; Selvini Palazzoli, 1974; Stern et al., 1981; White, 1983; Yager, 1982). Writings within the psychodynamic framework have portrayed other aspects of family psychological make-up. The work of Sours (1980) is especially relevant for the detailed evocation of the experience of such patients and the poetic title of his book on the subject (Starving to Death in a Sea of Objects) is a source for the title of this paper. The psychodynamic psychiatrist, Hilde Bruch (e.g. 1978), has also given vivid accounts of the internal world and its evolution in anorexic patients, accounts that have to be absorbed by the therapist wishing to engage with whole families in which there is an anorexic patient. All of these writings explore the development of the inner life of the patient by examining the anorexic patient's expression of their experience of relationships with parents.

In addition to using both family systems and psychoanalytic frameworks for understanding processes within and around the anorexic patient, there is another pertinent field: developing awareness of the psychological effects of starvation upon the individual (the effects of a starving child upon other family members must also be considered). This awareness is derived from studies now more than forty years old (Keys et al., 1948) showing that starvation produces clear psychological disturbances, some of which resemble aspects of anorexia nervosa: intense food preoccupation, hoarding food, making a meal last as long as possible by eating minute portions at a time, intense interest in food, cooking and the diet and weight of others, mood lability and depression, are all features of starvation in volunteers. For a fictional but highly accurate account of the effects of starvation on attitude to food, there is nothing more moving than that of A Day in the life of Ivan Denisovich (Solzhenitsyn, 1974).

Antonino Ferro. La tecnica in psicoanalisi infantile. II bambino e l'analista: dalla relazione al campo emotivo*. Milan: Cortina, 1992, 221 pages

Pierandrea Lussana

Pierandrea Lussana

Pierandrea Lussana  

This book's author is one of the fifteen analysts whose clinical accounts of psychoanalysis were published in Part 3/1991 of The International Journal of Psycho-Analysis. Trained at the Milan Institute of the Italian Psychoanalytical Society, he describes his theoretical orientation as Kleinian influenced by Bion.

In her Introduction to ‘The analysis of children’, Part Three, in Volume 2, Mainly Practice, of Melanie Klein Today (1988), E. Bott Spillius mentions that child analysis began to decline in the 1950s (with the notable exception of the work of Meltzer), experiencing something of a revival from the mid 1970s. For this reason it seems both useful and important to consider the development of child analysis in Italy, where Meltzer taught a great deal and where the influence of Bion's ideas is strong and has anything but well defined and predictable effects on the technique of Kleinian analysis. In ‘Notes on memory and desire’, which E. Bott Spillius places first among the ‘Developments in technique’ in Melanie Klein Today, Bion concludes:

“His interpretations should gain in force and conviction - both for himself and his patient - because they derive from the emotional experience with a unique individual and not from generalized theories imperfectly ‘remembered’.”

From the emotional experience with the child and the relationship with him, which always generates an emotional field, the interpretation is gradually constructed - as Dr. Ferro already maintains in the title of his forcefully written and courageous book.

The first chapter is entitled ‘A survey of the theoretical models’. Here, the author refers not only to the models of Freud, Klein and Bion but also to the most recent models of Meltzer and Rosenfeld (Impasse and Interpretation), describing “how the models live within me and how I have negotiated them up to the present day”. He notes that we have passed from repression (Freud) via splitting (M. Klein) - together with projective identification, which is closely bound up with splitting - to the container-contained interaction (Bion), in which the relationship with the other is central and work on the container takes priority over that on the contained. Bion's extension of splitting and projective identification implies that projective identifications are bidirectional, running both from patient to analyst and from analyst to patient, with primitive parts of the patient interacting with primitive parts of the analyst.

[[RunningHead]]

Psychodynamic Aspects of Failure-To-Thrive: A Case Study**

Ruth Selwyn

Ruth Selwyn

2 Edis Street
London, NW1 8LG

Ruth Selwyn  

Introduction

The principal theme of this paper concerns the relation between an infant's failure-to-thrive (hereafter referred to as FTT) and the capacity of the mother to be attentive to that infant (in the very specific senses which will be discussed). In the case that I will describe this capacity is determined partly by the mother's depression and partly by her marital problems.

FTT involves a failure to grow and gain weight either from birth or after a period of normal physical development There are standardized centile charts on which a child's growth can be compared with others of his age. Those who are consistently below the third centile in weight or have a reduction in growth weight are the ones who give rise to concern and might be diagnosed as FTT. The causes of FTT may be organic, non-organic or, more commonly, a mixture of the two. One feature which is common to all FTT cases, however, whether of organic or non-organic origin, is the occurrence of a feeding problem.

At this point we may usefully move on to examine several theoretical ideas which inform my work with children and parents and more specifically with FTT cases.

Melanie Klein (1952) said that the infant is a “human object related from birth”. Her view was that mental development started from the relationship between the instinctual needs of the baby, on the one hand, and the personality and caring capabilities of the mother, on the other. Winnicott (1965) defined the “good enough mother” in terms of her capacity for “maternal preoccupation”, which he considered to be a pre-condition for a baby's emotional and physical development. Bion (1962) termed this characteristic “reverie” and argued that its function was to “contain” the baby's undigested emotional and physical experiences.

These ideas, amongst others, were substantiated and elaborated when E. Bick introduced her method of direct mother-infant observation in the 1950s (Bick, 1964). Bick described how the mother's attention acts as a sort of “mental skin” which holds the baby's personality together (Bick, 1968). As M. Harris put it, “emotions at the most primitive level are rooted in bodily states and sensations, and by responding to her baby's signals the mother enables the baby to have meaningful experiences” (Harris, 1976).

[[RunningHead]]

Resistance in Child Psychoanalysis**

Jill Miller

Jill Miller

240 St Paul St., Suite 315
Denver, CO 80206 USA

Jill Miller  

Introduction

Resistance is an inevitable development in every analysis or psychoanalytic psychotherapy. The intensity and frequency varies, as does the therapist's counter response. It can engender frustration and a feeling that the patient is merely being stubborn or rejecting, especially when it is misunderstood or not seen as an expected component of the analytic process.

By resistance I am referring descriptively to elements in the patient which oppose the psychoanalytic process, specifically the engagement in a process which entails self-observation. The patients I will discuss are ones who have built up defences against self-reflection, rather than ones who do not have this capacity. They were all in five times weekly psychoanalysis, came to treatment and changed.

The concept of resistance was introduced by Freud and has remained a crucial component of psychoanalytic thinking. Following the introduction of the structural theory in 1923, he began to elaborate the idea of resistance. In Inhibitions, symptoms and anxiety (1926) he discussed five types of resistance, three of which originated in the ego, one in the id, and one in the superego. A decade later in The Ego and the Mechanisms of Defence Anna Freud (1936) expanded the concept. Resistances, she said, were an object of analytic study and provided useful information as to the patient's mental functioning. “Analysis of resistance could be seen as essentially the analysis of those aspects of the patient's defences which entered into and contributed to the pathological outcome of conflicts” (Sandler, Holder and Dare 1973, p. 77). In the classical sense resistance is conceptualised as a force which works against recollection and free association, keeping unconscious thoughts and phantasies from becoming conscious, thereby halting the flow of material. It is now seen to encompass all obstacles to the aims and processes of treatment which arise from within the patient.

Resistance develops during the course of every analysis and is related to transference and defences against anxiety-provoking material. Anna Freud thought the inability to carry out the conscious intent of working in analysis showed the resistance due to defences. Where there was no intent, the resistance couldn't be seen. She distinguished resistance from conscious withholding which was an opting out of the therapeutic contract.

[[RunningHead]]

How Far is near Enough? A Waiting Game

Niki Parker

Niki Parker

14 Gilkes Crescent
London SE21

Niki Parker  

Introduction

In this paper I describe once then twice a week therapy with Becky whom I met when she was fifteen. She presented with anorexia; after referral, bulimia, suicidal behaviour and a history of sexual abuse emerged. In looking for the meaning of her symptoms, I have had to look at her earliest experience as a feeding baby, when psychological and physiological aspects are virtually inseparable.

The development of early object relations and the nature of internalised objects were, I believe, critical for Becky, as was the way in which this process was influenced and modulated through a particular feeding experience. That this occurred for Becky in the context of a family with an inter-generational history of violence, neglect and lack of appropriate or protective boundaries added to the problems of developing an integrated sense of a self and healthy body ego. In this Becky differed from those adolescents presenting with anorexia, who appear to be seeking strategies of dealing with separation (cf. Dare 1993). She appears to be more typical of Lacey's (1993) core group of multi-impulsive bulimics whose self damaging and addictive behaviour has huge treatment implications. The trauma for Becky and the focus of her therapy was unsatisfactory attachment. This presented complications as the adolescent's main developmental task should be separation and individuation. Our heady therapeutic cocktail was shaken and stirred by a high capacity for acting out and dramatic swings between self destruction and a sense of hope. Counter-transference feelings were often my principal therapeutic tool: the idea of the mutative counter-transference was critical to our survival and progress.

Also of great importance has been the impact of the work with Becky and her family on the clinic team. We have found ourselves at times in dispute, at times in very atypical non-communication, always under seemingly great pressure to split and go in different ways. The impact of this was stressful and it took considerable effort on the part of our normally well-functioning team to remember our usual, preferred ways of working together. We concluded that we were responding to a powerful family/clinic countertransference and, at the times when communication seemed doomed, were ourselves replaying unhelpful family strategies for negotiating intimacy and change.

[[RunningHead]]

Feeding Problems and Relationship Difficulties: Therapeutic Work with Parents and Infants

Dilys Daws

Dilys Daws

120 Belsize Lane
London NW3 5BA

Dilys Daws  

Watching the behaviour of recently-born lambs and their ewe mothers one Easter on a Welsh hill-side, I saw the instinctive ‘homing-in’ by lambs to their mothers, and the searching and claiming by mothers of their offspring. Identifying at different times with one or the other, at one moment I was distressed when a lamb wandered bleating from one ewe to another, rebuffed by each one in turn; where was it's mother? At other moments I felt myself flinching as lambs hurled themselves on their mothers and roughly and imperiously rooted straight onto their nipples.

It is obvious from these examples that something was going on about feeding as a part of a mother-infant relationship that aroused strong emotional reactions, even in an uninvolved outside observer. My first reactions were often of empathy with one or other of the nursing couple. I hope that as a devotee of parent-infant work my ability to encompass both sides of the relationship was quickly mobilised. But it is relevant to point out that, in such an emotive area, any one of us can be drawn, without noticing it, to a one-sided view.

In this paper I will look at infant feeding, both by breast and by bottle, in the context of the development of the relationship between the infant and its mother and father. I will not generally be thinking about the infant on his or her own, whether in the context of successful feeding, or of problems in feeding that would seem to stem from deep disturbances in the infant. Crucial is what the infant's parents bring to the relationship from their experience and memories of being with their own parents. Carrying on this theme all ‘helpers’, such as doctors, nurses or health visitors trying to assist in establishing feeding, or psychotherapists stepping in at a later stage, may have attributed to them some aspect of the ideas about parents that these mothers and fathers have in their minds.

The subject of infant feeding is so fraught because it is literally a matter of life and death: an infant not fed sufficiently and appropriately dies. Even if the result is not quite so stark, but things are going pretty badly, the result is ‘failure to thrive’.

The Breast and Breasts

Serge Lebovici and Evelyne Kestemberg

Evelyne Kestemberg

Paris *
Universite Paris-Nord UFR Sante-Medicine-Biologie humaine 74, rue Marcel-Cachin 93012 Bobigny Cedex France

Evelyne Kestemberg  

Introduction

Is the breast taken into the mouth the same thing as both breasts as they are seen by the child? Taking the breast into the mouth by no means excludes the possibility of erotic pleasure for both parties as has been shown by a number of studies which suggest that the breast is no longer only the signifier of a so-called ‘partial’ object. This is what the iconography in sacred and profane love** confirms.

To speak of the breast, when one is a psychoanalyst, is to evoke oral fixations, often to think in terms of the theories of Melanie Klein or of her successors. But it is also, and most frequently, to neglect this female organ itself, which constitutes for both sexes a source of pleasure. My experience with babies and their mothers has frequently borne this out, for breast-feeding is a source of enjoyment equally for both parties.

First of all 1 shall present in some detail a case history which poses certain problems in this regard. I shall then try, in this paper, to bring together into a more unified concept the breast as a symbol of maternity, and the breasts as an object of lust for some and a source of pleasure for others.

A Breast for Two or for Three?1

Douce is a baby who will be seen twice, at five months and at eleven months, with sleeping problems: she cannot go to sleep except with her mother's breast in her mouth.

Of the mother, known to the observer, it is sufficient to say that she has had a child by a father who has refused paternity. She wanted to prove that she would have a child who would grow up free and who would choose her own time for taking the breast. It is important to bear in mind at this point that the maternal grandmother died of breast cancer.

The two consultations were each preceded by a long letter, which the

Heroic Deeds, Manic Defence and Intrusive Identification: Some Reflections on Psychotherapy with a 16-Year Old Boy**

Miranda Davies

Miranda Davies

53 Marlborough Crescent
Bedford Park
London W4 1HG

Miranda Davies  

In this paper I should like to look at a particular aspect of adolescence, that is, the heroic stance as a defence against impotence, helplessness, dependency and depression. I propose to link the heroic flight into action with a particularly active and intrusive use of projective identification by my young patient. Projective identification was first defined by Melanie Klein. In “Notes on some schizoid mechanisms” she described a process of projective identification in which parts of the ego are forced into another's psyche in order to take over its contents or to control it (Klein 1946). This is a deeply unconscious process motivated by envy, and the result is a depletion of the subject and weakened sense of self and identity.

As an analytical psychologist, Michael Fordham was not working with the same model of the psyche as Klein. Nevertheless, he found her discoveries of the working of unconscious phantasy in children to be inspiring, and her descriptions of her clinical work helped him to gain direct access to the unconscious of his own child patients. He writes, “I recognised that what she wrote might be a basis for developing a Jungian understanding of child development” (Fordham 1989). Klein, following Susan Isaacs, distinguished between two kinds of fantasy: conscious fantasy that is directly accessible in daydreams and, for Jungians, in active imagination, and unconscious phantasy that is the psychic pattern that underlies instinctual activity. Two spellings of the word are used by Kleinians to help the reader recognise the distinction between conscious fantasy and unconscious phantasy and I shall follow this practice. Fordham regards Klein as one of his mentors, and the close correspondence between unconscious phantasy and archetypal patterns was the basis from which he extended Jung's idea of the self and individuation to apply to infancy and childhood. For this reason, the training in child analysis in London under Fordham's direction has assimilated a number of Klein's ideas, but within the context of Jung's model of the psyche.

[[RunningHead]]

Valerie Sinason. Mental Handicap and the Human Condition. New Approaches from the Tavistock. Published by Free Association Books, 1992. Paperback, £19.95.

Peter Fonagy

Peter Fonagy

Peter Fonagy  

It is rare to have the opportunity to review a book which deserves unqualified praise. Valerie Sinason's book, which summarises her work over the past ten years in psychodynamic treatment of individuals with learning difficulties, is that relatively unusual volume which advances practice and theory at the same time as transfixing the reader, compelling him/her to read on to hear about the next interpretation, the next session, the next case. It represents a milestone in psychoanalytically-oriented understanding of this extremely complex group of patients, as well as representing a major development and extension of the clinical domain of psychotherapeutic practice.

Valerie Sinason makes a major theoretical contribution in identifying important aspects of our subjective reactions to individuals labelled ‘stupid’, ‘mentally handicapped’, or ‘experiencing learning difficulties’. She understands and is sympathetic to our struggle with the stupid parts of ourselves, and illustrates how social structures come to our aid to buttress our fragile selves and prevent us from fully accepting the reality of the truth of impaired cognition. She is quite brilliant in tracing the processes of euphemism and linguistic acrobatics put in the service of avoidance and denial of knowledge about this group. She tracks it to our inability to deal with difference without guilt or envy, whilst highlighting the closeness of euphemism and abuse.

Valerie Sinason is not the first person to have worked with this group of patients, as her highly informative review acknowledges. Her short history of work in this area offers a very balanced coverage of previous work. It is, however, the case studies, the second part of this exciting book, which make this volume such a special one. For me it opened a window on a world which I had but the vaguest and, if I am honest, the most distorted, ideas about before reading the book. Reading these cases is a liberating experience; the treatments convey the human tragedy of handicap whilst making real the possibility of contact and understanding. The author guides her patients and her reader sensitively and lyrically through the subjective world of individuals starved of love and affection and who daily confront false concern disguising deep hatred. She shows how the handicapped smile so often disguises intense pain, the body attempting to make a self-effacing apology for the mind within.
